title: continuous-batcher: scheduler tuning for queueing fairness, starvation prevention, and timeouts
author: Sofia Nguyen
description:
Context: The continuous-batcher scheduler has been observed to favor large batch formation in high-concurrency workloads, which can cause long-tail latency regressions and request starvation for low-volume models. This PR implements a set of scheduler tunings intended to improve queueing fairness, prevent starvation, and bound worst-case queue latency.

What this changes: 1) Request aging: each queued request now accrues an "age" score that increases linearly while waiting. The scheduler uses (base_priority + age * aging_factor) when selecting candidates for batch formation so older requests gradually win over bulky low-priority traffic. 2) Per-model fairness windows: the scheduler tracks a moving-window token budget for each model to prevent a single hot model from monopolizing batching slots. Tokens refill at a configurable rate. 3) Max-queue-timeouts: a per-request max_wait_ms is enforced at the scheduler layer (default 120ms for interactive workloads). Requests that hit max_wait_ms are forced into a smaller immediate batch or are routed to a low-latency fallback path. 4) Backpressure signaling: when queues grow beyond alert thresholds we emit new scheduler-level metrics and a brief backpressure hint to frontends so routing can shift to heavier throughput nodes. 5) KV-cache interaction: we adjusted KV cache prefetch heuristics to avoid prefetch churn for requests that are about to be forced by max-queue-timeouts; this reduces wasted cache work. 6) Safe defaults & config: added runtime flags and config knobs (aging_factor, token_rate, max_wait_ms, fairness_window_ms) and documented recommended settings.

Why: These changes target production symptoms reported in ENG-1042 and ENG-1109: P99 spikes under mixed workloads, and long wait times for small-volume/premium traffic. The approach is conservative - defaults improve fairness while minimizing throughput regression.

Checklist: - [x] Scheduler logic implemented and unit-tested - [x] Integration tests for mixed-model workloads added - [x] Benchmarks (micro & mixed) added and ran on perf lab - [x] Metrics added for aging, token usage, forced-timeout counts - [x] Docs and config examples updated - [x] Rollback plan: feature guarded by cluster flag and config; revert is a single-commit config flip.

Testing & Results: Microbenchmarks on perf-canary show: - P50: +0-1% (statistically neutral) - P95: -4% latency on mixed read/write prompt mixes - P99: -9% to -13% latency reduction depending on model mix (most improvement when one hot model previously dominated) - Throughput: -1% to +4% depending on workload (net-neutral; some small throughput regressions when aggressive aging is enabled)

Notes: The default max_wait_ms is conservative for interactive workloads; infra teams may tune per-customer. The PR intentionally does not change model selection/routing policies beyond the fairness token accounting; larger routing changes are tracked in a follow-up.

release_notes: Improved continuous-batcher scheduler fairness and reduced P99 latency for mixed workloads by adding request aging, per-model fairness tokens, and bounded queue timeouts. Added metrics and tuning knobs. Default settings are conservative to avoid throughput regressions.
performance_summary: Mixed-workload perf lab: P95 -4%, P99 -9%..-13% (depends on model mix), throughput +/-4% (config-dependent); small improvements in per-request latency variance; observed elimination of starvation for low-volume traffic in simulated scenarios.
rollback_plan: Feature is behind a cluster-level flag. To roll back, flip 'scheduler.enable_fairness_v2' to false and revert the single commit that enables the flag in the deployment manifest. Detailed steps in docs/observability/scheduler.md.
notes: This PR is intentionally conservative: it focuses on scheduler-level fairness only. Routing-level traffic-shifts and model pinning changes are tracked separately (ENG-1167). Operators can tune aging_factor and max_wait_ms per class of traffic.
